claims.text: HEA coatings can provide wear-resistant surface protection.
Introducing a thin, graded Ni-based interfacial layer between Cu and an HEA coating will improve interfacial bonding.
Improved interfacial bonding from the Ni-based layer will enhance the wear performance of the coated Cu component.
Direct deposition of an HEA coating on Cu can produce interfacial problems because of thermal-property mismatch.
Direct deposition of an HEA coating on Cu can produce interfacial problems because of crystallographic mismatch.
A graded Ni or Ni-Cr interlayer can be deposited on Cu by sputtering or laser cladding before applying an HEA coating.
High-energy coating processes require an interface with metallurgical bonding and thermal stability.
A graded interfacial layer will chemically bond to both the Cu substrate and the HEA coating.
The graded interfacial layer will bridge lattice mismatch between Cu and the HEA coating.
The graded interfacial layer will bridge thermal-expansion mismatch between Cu and the HEA coating.
A Ni-based interlayer will form a metallurgical bond with the Cu substrate.
A Ni-based interlayer will provide a surface compatible with the HEA coating.
The Ni-based interlayer will promote diffusion bonding at the coating-substrate interface.
Reduced mismatch and enhanced diffusion bonding will decrease delamination under tribological loading.
Reduced mismatch and enhanced diffusion bonding will decrease cracking under tribological loading.
The interlayer-modified coating will have greater adhesion, durability, and wear resistance than an HEA coating deposited directly on Cu.
The adhesion benefit depends on optimization of interlayer composition, thickness, grading, and processing parameters.
An interlayer that is too thick, too thin, or improperly graded may provide diminished benefits.
Extreme thermal cycling may impair the long-term stability of the modified interface.
Interfacial engineering usually enhances bonding.
